import Foundation.FirstOrder.Basic.Operator
import Foundation.FirstOrder.Basic.Semantics.Elementary

namespace LO

namespace FirstOrder

namespace Structure

structure Model (L : Language) (M : Type*) :=
  intro : M

namespace Model

variable [Structure L M]

def equiv (L : Language) (M : Type*) : M ≃ Model L M where
  toFun := fun x => ⟨x⟩
  invFun := Model.intro
  left_inv := by intro x; simp
  right_inv := by rintro ⟨x⟩; simp

instance : Structure L (Model L M) := Structure.ofEquiv (equiv L M)

instance [h : Nonempty M] : Nonempty (Model L M) := by
  rcases h with ⟨x⟩; exact ⟨equiv L M x⟩

lemma elementaryEquiv (L : Language) (M : Type*) [Nonempty M] [Structure L M] : M ≡ₑ[L] Model L M :=
  ElementaryEquiv.ofEquiv _

section

open Semiterm Semiformula

instance [Operator.Zero L] : Zero (Model L M) := ⟨(@Operator.Zero.zero L _).val ![]⟩

instance [Operator.Zero L] : Structure.Zero L (Model L M) := ⟨rfl⟩

instance [Operator.One L] : One (Model L M) := ⟨(@Operator.One.one L _).val ![]⟩

instance [Operator.One L] : Structure.One L (Model L M) := ⟨rfl⟩

instance [Operator.Add L] : Add (Model L M) :=
  ⟨fun x y => (@Operator.Add.add L _).val ![x, y]⟩

instance [Operator.Add L] : Structure.Add L (Model L M) := ⟨fun _ _ => rfl⟩

instance [Operator.Mul L] : Mul (Model L M) :=
  ⟨fun x y => (@Operator.Mul.mul L _).val ![x, y]⟩

instance [Operator.Mul L] : Structure.Mul L (Model L M) := ⟨fun _ _ => rfl⟩

instance [Operator.Exp L] : Exp (Model L M) :=
  ⟨fun x => (@Operator.Exp.exp L _).val ![x]⟩

instance [Operator.Exp L] : Structure.Exp L (Model L M) := ⟨fun _ => rfl⟩

instance [Operator.Eq L] [Structure.Eq L M] : Structure.Eq L (Model L M) :=
  ⟨fun x y => by simp [operator_val_ofEquiv_iff]⟩

instance [Operator.LT L] : LT (Model L M) :=
  ⟨fun x y => (@Operator.LT.lt L _).val ![x, y]⟩

instance [Operator.LT L] : Structure.LT L (Model L M) := ⟨fun _ _ => iff_of_eq rfl⟩

instance [Operator.Mem L] : Membership (Model L M) (Model L M) :=
  ⟨fun x y => (@Operator.Mem.mem L _).val ![y, x]⟩

instance [Operator.Mem L] : Structure.Mem L (Model L M) := ⟨fun _ _ => iff_of_eq rfl⟩

end

end Model

section ofFunc

variable (F : ℕ → Type*) {M : Type*} (fF : {k : ℕ} → (f : F k) → (Fin k → M) → M)

def ofFunc : Structure (Language.ofFunc F) M where
  func := fun _ f v => fF f v
  rel  := fun _ r _ => r.elim

lemma func_ofFunc {k} (f : F k) (v : Fin k → M) : (ofFunc F fF).func f v = fF f v := rfl

end ofFunc

section add

variable (L₁ : Language.{u₁}) (L₂ : Language.{u₂}) (M : Type*) [str₁ : Structure L₁ M] [str₂ : Structure L₂ M]

instance add : Structure (L₁.add L₂) M where
  func := fun _ f v =>
    match f with
    | Sum.inl f => func f v
    | Sum.inr f => func f v
  rel := fun _ r v =>
    match r with
    | Sum.inl r => rel r v
    | Sum.inr r => rel r v

variable {L₁ L₂ M}

@[simp] lemma func_sigma_inl {k} (f : L₁.Func k) (v : Fin k → M) :
    (add L₁ L₂ M).func (Sum.inl f) v = func f v := rfl

@[simp] lemma func_sigma_inr {k} (f : L₂.Func k) (v : Fin k → M) :
    (add L₁ L₂ M).func (Sum.inr f) v = func f v := rfl

@[simp] lemma rel_sigma_inl {k} (r : L₁.Rel k) (v : Fin k → M) :
    (add L₁ L₂ M).rel (Sum.inl r) v ↔ rel r v := iff_of_eq rfl

@[simp] lemma rel_sigma_inr {k} (r : L₂.Rel k) (v : Fin k → M) :
    (add L₁ L₂ M).rel (Sum.inr r) v ↔ rel r v := iff_of_eq rfl

@[simp] lemma val_lMap_add₁ {n} (t : Semiterm L₁ μ n) (e : Fin n → M) (ε : μ → M) :
    Semiterm.val (add L₁ L₂ M) e ε (t.lMap (Language.Hom.add₁ L₁ L₂)) = t.val str₁ e ε := by
  induction t <;> simp [Semiterm.lMap_func, Semiterm.val, Language.Hom.func_add₁, *]

@[simp] lemma val_lMap_add₂ {n} (t : Semiterm L₂ μ n) (e : Fin n → M) (ε : μ → M) :
    Semiterm.val (add L₁ L₂ M) e ε (t.lMap (Language.Hom.add₂ L₁ L₂)) = t.val str₂ e ε := by
  induction t <;> simp [Semiterm.lMap_func, Semiterm.val, Language.Hom.func_add₂, *]

@[simp] lemma eval_lMap_add₁ {n} (φ : Semiformula L₁ μ n) (e : Fin n → M) (ε : μ → M) :
    Semiformula.Eval (add L₁ L₂ M) e ε (Semiformula.lMap (Language.Hom.add₁ L₁ L₂) φ)
    ↔ Semiformula.Eval str₁ e ε φ := by
  induction φ using Semiformula.rec' <;>
    simp [*, Language.Hom.rel_add₁, Semiformula.eval_rel,
      Semiformula.lMap_rel, Semiformula.eval_nrel, Semiformula.lMap_nrel]

@[simp] lemma eval_lMap_add₂ {n} (φ : Semiformula L₂ μ n) (e : Fin n → M) (ε : μ → M) :
    Semiformula.Eval (add L₁ L₂ M) e ε (Semiformula.lMap (Language.Hom.add₂ L₁ L₂) φ)
    ↔ Semiformula.Eval str₂ e ε φ := by
  induction φ using Semiformula.rec' <;>
    simp [*, Language.Hom.rel_add₂, Semiformula.eval_rel,
      Semiformula.lMap_rel, Semiformula.eval_nrel, Semiformula.lMap_nrel]

end add

section sigma

variable (L : ι → Language) (M : Type*) [str : (i : ι) → Structure (L i) M]

instance sigma : Structure (Language.sigma L) M where
  func := fun _ ⟨_, f⟩ v => func f v
  rel  := fun _ ⟨_, r⟩ v => rel r v

@[simp] lemma func_sigma {k} (f : (L i).Func k) (v : Fin k → M) : (sigma L M).func ⟨i, f⟩ v = func f v := rfl

    Semiterm.val (sigma L M) e ε (t.lMap (Language.Hom.sigma L i)) = t.val (str i) e ε := by

@[simp] lemma eval_lMap_sigma {n} (φ : Semiformula (L i) μ n) (e : Fin n → M) (ε : μ → M) :
    Semiformula.Eval (sigma L M) e ε (Semiformula.lMap (Language.Hom.sigma L i) φ)
    ↔ Semiformula.Eval (str i) e ε φ := by
  induction φ using Semiformula.rec' <;>
    simp [*, Language.Hom.rel_sigma, Semiformula.eval_rel,
      Semiformula.lMap_rel, Semiformula.eval_nrel, Semiformula.lMap_nrel]

end sigma

end Structure

section ULift

variable {L : Language.{u}} {M : Type v} [Structure L M]

instance : Structure L (ULift.{v'} M) where
  func := fun _ f v ↦ ⟨Structure.func f fun i ↦ (v i).down⟩
  rel := fun _ r v ↦ Structure.rel r fun i ↦ (v i).down

    Structure.func f v = ⟨Structure.func f fun i ↦ (v i).down⟩ := rfl

    Structure.rel r v = Structure.rel r fun i ↦ (v i).down := rfl

lemma Semiterm.valm_uLift {e : Fin n → ULift.{v'} M} {ε : ξ → ULift.{v'} M} {t : Semiterm L ξ n} :
    Semiterm.valm (ULift.{v'} M) e ε t = ⟨Semiterm.valm M (fun i ↦ (e i).down) (fun i ↦ (ε i).down) t⟩ := by
  induction t <;> simp [*, Semiterm.val_func]

lemma Semiformula.evalm_uLift {e : Fin n → ULift.{v'} M} {ε : ξ → ULift.{v'} M} {φ : Semiformula L ξ n} :
    Semiformula.Evalm (ULift.{v'} M) e ε φ ↔ Semiformula.Evalm M (fun i ↦ (e i).down) (fun i ↦ (ε i).down) φ := by
  induction φ using Semiformula.rec' <;>
    simp [*, Semiformula.eval_rel, Semiformula.eval_nrel, Semiterm.valm_uLift, Matrix.comp_vecCons']

lemma uLift_elementaryEquiv [Nonempty M] : ULift.{v'} M ≡ₑ[L] M := by

  toFun := fun x => ⟨x⟩
  invFun := Model.intro
  left_inv := by intro x; simp

instance : Structure L (Model L M) := Structure.ofEquiv (equiv L M)

instance [h : Nonempty M] : Nonempty (Model L M) := by
  rcases h with ⟨x⟩; exact ⟨equiv L M x⟩

lemma elementaryEquiv (L : Language) (M : Type*) [Nonempty M] [Structure L M] : M ≡ₑ[L] Model L M :=
  ElementaryEquiv.ofEquiv _

@[elab_as_elim]
def rec' {C : ∀ n, Semiformula L ξ n → Sort w}
  (hverum  : ∀ {n : ℕ}, C n ⊤)
  (hfalsum : ∀ {n : ℕ}, C n ⊥)
  (hrel    : ∀ {n k : ℕ} (r : L.Rel k) (v : Fin k → Semiterm L ξ n), C n (rel r v))
  (hnrel   : ∀ {n k : ℕ} (r : L.Rel k) (v : Fin k → Semiterm L ξ n), C n (nrel r v))
  (hand    : ∀ {n : ℕ} (φ ψ : Semiformula L ξ n), C n φ → C n ψ → C n (φ ⋏ ψ))
  (hor     : ∀ {n : ℕ} (φ ψ : Semiformula L ξ n), C n φ → C n ψ → C n (φ ⋎ ψ))
  (hall    : ∀ {n : ℕ} (φ : Semiformula L ξ (n + 1)), C (n + 1) φ → C n (∀' φ))
  (hex     : ∀ {n : ℕ} (φ : Semiformula L ξ (n + 1)), C (n + 1) φ → C n (∃' φ)) :
    ∀ {n : ℕ} (φ : Semiformula L ξ n), C n φ
  | _, verum    => hverum
  | _, falsum   => hfalsum
  | _, rel r v  => hrel r v
  | _, nrel r v => hnrel r v
  | _, and φ ψ  => hand φ ψ (rec' hverum hfalsum hrel hnrel hand hor hall hex φ) (rec' hverum hfalsum hrel hnrel hand hor hall hex ψ)
  | _, or φ ψ   => hor φ ψ (rec' hverum hfalsum hrel hnrel hand hor hall hex φ) (rec' hverum hfalsum hrel hnrel hand hor hall hex ψ)
  | _, all φ    => hall φ (rec' hverum hfalsum hrel hnrel hand hor hall hex φ)
  | _, ex φ     => hex φ (rec' hverum hfalsum hrel hnrel hand hor hall hex φ)

  (hor     : ∀ {n : ℕ} (φ ψ : Semiformula L ξ n), C n φ → C n ψ → C n (φ ⋎ ψ))
  (hall    : ∀ {n : ℕ} (φ : Semiformula L ξ (n + 1)), C (n + 1) φ → C n (∀' φ))
  (hex     : ∀ {n : ℕ} (φ : Semiformula L ξ (n + 1)), C (n + 1) φ → C n (∃' φ)) :
    ∀ {n : ℕ} (φ : Semiformula L ξ n), C n φ
  | _, verum    => hverum
  | _, falsum   => hfalsum
  | _, rel r v  => hrel r v
  | _, nrel r v => hnrel r v
  | _, and φ ψ  => hand φ ψ (rec' hverum hfalsum hrel hnrel hand hor hall hex φ) (rec' hverum hfalsum hrel hnrel hand hor hall hex ψ)
  | _, or φ ψ   => hor φ ψ (rec' hverum hfalsum hrel hnrel hand hor hall hex φ) (rec' hverum hfalsum hrel hnrel hand hor hall hex ψ)
  | _, all φ    => hall φ (rec' hverum hfalsum hrel hnrel hand hor hall hex φ)
  | _, ex φ     => hex φ (rec' hverum hfalsum hrel hnrel hand hor hall hex φ)

structure Model (L : Language) (M : Type*) :=

variable [Structure L M]

def equiv (L : Language) (M : Type*) : M ≃ Model L M where
  toFun := fun x => ⟨x⟩
  invFun := Model.intro
  left_inv := by intro x; simp
  right_inv := by rintro ⟨x⟩; simp

instance : Structure L (Model L M) := Structure.ofEquiv (equiv L M)

instance [h : Nonempty M] : Nonempty (Model L M) := by
  rcases h with ⟨x⟩; exact ⟨equiv L M x⟩

lemma elementaryEquiv (L : Language) (M : Type*) [Nonempty M] [Structure L M] : M ≡ₑ[L] Model L M :=
  ElementaryEquiv.ofEquiv _

C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

C1_dependencies.name: rfl
C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a
C1_dependencies.compilationAlias:

@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

C1_dependencies.name: rfl
C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

structure Model (L : Language) (M : Type*) :=

def rec' {C : ∀ n, Semiformula L ξ n → Sort w}
  (hverum  : ∀ {n : ℕ}, C n ⊤)
  (hfalsum : ∀ {n : ℕ}, C n ⊥)
  (hrel    : ∀ {n k : ℕ} (r : L.Rel k) (v : Fin k → Semiterm L ξ n), C n (rel r v))
  (hnrel   : ∀ {n k : ℕ} (r : L.Rel k) (v : Fin k → Semiterm L ξ n), C n (nrel r v))
  (hand    : ∀ {n : ℕ} (φ ψ : Semiformula L ξ n), C n φ → C n ψ → C n (φ ⋏ ψ))
  (hor     : ∀ {n : ℕ} (φ ψ : Semiformula L ξ n), C n φ → C n ψ → C n (φ ⋎ ψ))
  (hall    : ∀ {n : ℕ} (φ : Semiformula L ξ (n + 1)), C (n + 1) φ → C n (∀' φ))
  (hex     : ∀ {n : ℕ} (φ : Semiformula L ξ (n + 1)), C (n + 1) φ → C n (∃' φ)) :
    ∀ {n : ℕ} (φ : Semiformula L ξ n), C n φ
  | _, verum    => hverum
  | _, falsum   => hfalsum
  | _, rel r v  => hrel r v
  | _, nrel r v => hnrel r v
  | _, and φ ψ  => hand φ ψ (rec' hverum hfalsum hrel hnrel hand hor hall hex φ) (rec' hverum hfalsum hrel hnrel hand hor hall hex ψ)
  | _, or φ ψ   => hor φ ψ (rec' hverum hfalsum hrel hnrel hand hor hall hex φ) (rec' hverum hfalsum hrel hnrel hand hor hall hex ψ)
  | _, all φ    => hall φ (rec' hverum hfalsum hrel hnrel hand hor hall hex φ)
  | _, ex φ     => hex φ (rec' hverum hfalsum hrel hnrel hand hor hall hex φ)

import Foundation.FirstOrder.Basic.Operator
import Foundation.FirstOrder.Basic.Semantics.Elementary

namespace LO

namespace FirstOrder

namespace Structure

structure Model (L : Language) (M : Type*) :=
  intro : M

namespace Model

variable [Structure L M]

def equiv (L : Language) (M : Type*) : M ≃ Model L M where
  toFun := fun x => ⟨x⟩
  invFun := Model.intro
  left_inv := by intro x; simp
  right_inv := by rintro ⟨x⟩; simp

instance : Structure L (Model L M) := Structure.ofEquiv (equiv L M)

instance [h : Nonempty M] : Nonempty (Model L M) := by
  rcases h with ⟨x⟩; exact ⟨equiv L M x⟩

lemma elementaryEquiv (L : Language) (M : Type*) [Nonempty M] [Structure L M] : M ≡ₑ[L] Model L M :=
  ElementaryEquiv.ofEquiv _

section

open Semiterm Semiformula

instance [Operator.Zero L] : Zero (Model L M) := ⟨(@Operator.Zero.zero L _).val ![]⟩

instance [Operator.Zero L] : Structure.Zero L (Model L M) := ⟨rfl⟩

instance [Operator.One L] : One (Model L M) := ⟨(@Operator.One.one L _).val ![]⟩

instance [Operator.One L] : Structure.One L (Model L M) := ⟨rfl⟩

instance [Operator.Add L] : Add (Model L M) :=
  ⟨fun x y => (@Operator.Add.add L _).val ![x, y]⟩

instance [Operator.Add L] : Structure.Add L (Model L M) := ⟨fun _ _ => rfl⟩

instance [Operator.Mul L] : Mul (Model L M) :=
  ⟨fun x y => (@Operator.Mul.mul L _).val ![x, y]⟩

instance [Operator.Mul L] : Structure.Mul L (Model L M) := ⟨fun _ _ => rfl⟩

instance [Operator.Exp L] : Exp (Model L M) :=
  ⟨fun x => (@Operator.Exp.exp L _).val ![x]⟩

instance [Operator.Exp L] : Structure.Exp L (Model L M) := ⟨fun _ => rfl⟩

instance [Operator.Eq L] [Structure.Eq L M] : Structure.Eq L (Model L M) :=
  ⟨fun x y => by simp [operator_val_ofEquiv_iff]⟩

instance [Operator.LT L] : LT (Model L M) :=
  ⟨fun x y => (@Operator.LT.lt L _).val ![x, y]⟩

instance [Operator.LT L] : Structure.LT L (Model L M) := ⟨fun _ _ => iff_of_eq rfl⟩

instance [Operator.Mem L] : Membership (Model L M) (Model L M) :=
  ⟨fun x y => (@Operator.Mem.mem L _).val ![y, x]⟩

instance [Operator.Mem L] : Structure.Mem L (Model L M) := ⟨fun _ _ => iff_of_eq rfl⟩

end

end Model

section ofFunc

variable (F : ℕ → Type*) {M : Type*} (fF : {k : ℕ} → (f : F k) → (Fin k → M) → M)

def ofFunc : Structure (Language.ofFunc F) M where
  func := fun _ f v => fF f v
  rel  := fun _ r _ => r.elim

lemma func_ofFunc {k} (f : F k) (v : Fin k → M) : (ofFunc F fF).func f v = fF f v := rfl

end ofFunc

section add

variable (L₁ : Language.{u₁}) (L₂ : Language.{u₂}) (M : Type*) [str₁ : Structure L₁ M] [str₂ : Structure L₂ M]

instance add : Structure (L₁.add L₂) M where
  func := fun _ f v =>
    match f with
    | Sum.inl f => func f v
    | Sum.inr f => func f v
  rel := fun _ r v =>
    match r with
    | Sum.inl r => rel r v
    | Sum.inr r => rel r v

variable {L₁ L₂ M}

    (add L₁ L₂ M).func (Sum.inl f) v = func f v := rfl

    Semiterm.val (add L₁ L₂ M) e ε (t.lMap (Language.Hom.add₁ L₁ L₂)) = t.val str₁ e ε := by
  induction t <;> simp [Semiterm.lMap_func, Semiterm.val, Language.Hom.func_add₁, *]

  induction t <;> simp [Semiterm.lMap_func, Semiterm.val, Language.Hom.func_add₂, *]

C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

structure Model (L : Language) (M : Type*) :=
  intro : M

variable [Structure L M]

  toFun := fun x => ⟨x⟩
  invFun := Model.intro

instance [h : Nonempty M] : Nonempty (Model L M) := by
  rcases h with ⟨x⟩; exact ⟨equiv L M x⟩

  ElementaryEquiv.ofEquiv _

C1_dependencies.name: rfl
C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

First, consider a non-empty set `M`. The construction `uLift.{v'} M` creates a lifted version of `M` within a higher universe. To establish elementary equivalence, we need to show that any first-order statement true in `M` remains true in `uLift.{v'} M`, and conversely, any such statement true in `uLift.{v'} M` is also true in `M`.

To demonstrate this, we employ a back-and-forth argument, which is a standard technique in model theory for establishing elementary equivalence. This approach involves defining a sequence of mappings that preserve the truth of all first-order formulas.

1. **Forward Direction**:
   - Assume a first-order formula `φ` holds in `uLift.{v'} M`. By the definition of lifting and the properties of elementary equivalence, there exists a corresponding formula `φ'` in the original structure `M` that reflects the satisfaction of `φ`. Since `φ` holds in `uLift.{v'} M`, `φ'` must hold in `M`.

2. **Reverse Direction**:
   - Conversely, if a first-order formula `φ` holds in `M`, the lifting process ensures that the formula `φ'` (which corresponds to `φ` in `uLift.{v'} M`) also holds in `uLift.{v'} M`. This follows from the inherent preservation of truth across lifted structures.

By constructing such a sequence of mappings and utilizing the properties of first-order logic, we establish that the lifted structure `uLift.{v'} M` and the original structure `M` are elementarily equivalent. This holds for any non-empty set `M`, thereby completing the proof.

C1_dependencies.name: rfl
C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

informal_statement: For any assignments \( e \) and \( \varepsilon \), the evaluation of a semiformula \( \varphi \) in the lifted model \( \mathbb{U}\text{Lift} \) is equivalent to the evaluation of \( \varphi \) in the original model \( M \) after applying the \( \text{down} \) function to \( e \) and \( \varepsilon \).
informal_proof:
To establish this equivalence, we will perform an inductive proof on the structure of the semiformula \( \varphi \). 

1. **Base Case**: When \( \varphi \) is an atomic semiformula, the evaluation in the lifted model directly corresponds to the evaluation in the original model. By applying the \( \text{down} \) function to the assignments \( e \) and \( \varepsilon \), we ensure that all values are projected back to the original model \( M \). Thus, the equivalence holds for atomic formulas.

2. **Inductive Step**: Assume that the equivalence holds for all semiformulas of a certain complexity. We need to show that it also holds for formulas formed by negation, conjunction, and universal quantification.

   - **Negation**: If \( \varphi \) is negated, the evaluation in the lifted model reflects the negation of the evaluated subformula. Similarly, in the original model, applying \( \text{down} \) ensures the evaluation corresponds correctly to the negation. Hence, the equivalence holds for negations.
   
   - **Conjunction**: If \( \varphi \) is a conjunction, the evaluation in the lifted model checks the truth of both subformulas. After applying \( \text{down} \), the evaluation in the original model aligns with this conjunction, maintaining equivalence.
   
   - **Universal Quantification**: For universally quantified formulas, the evaluation in the lifted model requires that all interpretations satisfy the subformula. By applying \( \text{down} \) to the assignments, the original model reflects all interpretations, ensuring the equivalence holds.

By induction, the equivalence between evaluating \( \varphi \) in \( \mathbb{U}\text{Lift} \) and in \( M \) after applying \( \text{down} \) holds for all semiformulas \( \varphi \).

open LO.FirstOrder.Semiterm LO.FirstOrder.Semiformula

variable [Structure L M]
informal_statement: For any semiterm \( t \) constructed from functions and variables, the valuation of \( t \) in a lifted model \( \mathcal{L}' \) is equal to the valuation in the original model \( \mathcal{L} \) of the corresponding lifted functions.
informal_proof:
We prove this statement by induction on the structure of the semiterm \( t \).

**Base Case:**  
If \( t \) is a variable, then the valuation in \( \mathcal{L}' \) is simply the interpretation of the variable in \( \mathcal{L}' \), which is equivalent to the interpretation of the lifted variable in \( \mathcal{L} \).

**Inductive Step:**  
Assume the statement holds for all subterms of \( t \). If \( t \) is constructed using a function symbol \( f \), then the valuation in \( \mathcal{L}' \) is determined by the valuations of its arguments, which by induction hypothesis are equal to their valuations in \( \mathcal{L} \). Since \( f' \) is the lift of \( f \), the resulting valuation in \( \mathcal{L}' \) matches the valuation in \( \mathcal{L} \).

Thus, by induction, the equality holds for all semiterms \( t \).

C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

<STATEMENT>

For any relation `r` on an indexed type `k`, the relation applied to an indexed family `v` is the same as the pointwise application of the relation `r` to the down-projected elements of `v`.

</STATEMENT>

<PROOF>

Given a relation `r` on an indexed type `k`, we aim to show that applying `r` to an indexed family `v` is equivalent to applying `r` pointwise to the down-projected elements of `v`.

First, consider the definition of `Structure.rel r v`, which operates on the indexed family `v`. By applying `r` to `v`, we obtain a relation defined by the indexed family of `r` applied to each element of `v`.

On the other hand, `Structure.rel r fun i ↦ (v i).down` involves projecting each element of `v` down to the underlying set before applying `r`. This results in a relation defined by the indexed family of `r` applied to the down-projected elements.

Since both expressions involve applying `r` in a pointwise manner to `v`, albeit interpreted differently in their respective contexts, the two relations are equivalent by the nature of how `r` interacts with the indexed family `v`. Thus, we conclude that:

\[
\text{Structure.rel } r\, v \; = \; \text{Structure.rel } r \; \left(\lambda i\, \mapsto\, (v\, i).down\right)
\]

Similarly, for the universal quantifier, we use the inductive hypothesis to establish that the equivalence holds for all elements in the domain, thereby confirming the equivalence for the universally quantified formula.

C1_dependencies.name: rfl
C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

C1_dependencies.name: rfl
C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a
C1_dependencies.compilationAlias:

the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

C1_dependencies.name: rfl
C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

informal_statement: When we add two linear maps \( L_1 \) and \( L_2 \) to another linear map or structure and subsequently apply a function that focuses on a particular component \( f \), the result is equivalent to applying \( f \) directly without considering the addition of \( L_1 \) and \( L_2 \).
informal_proof:
To understand and prove the statement, let's break down the components involved and analyze their interactions step by step.

1. **Linear Maps and Their Sum**: 
   - Consider two linear maps \( L_1 \) and \( L_2 \) that operate on a vector space \( V \).
   - The sum of these linear maps, denoted as \( L_1 + L_2 \), is defined such that for any vector \( v \) in \( V \):
     \[
     (L_1 + L_2)(v) = L_1(v) + L_2(v)
     \]
     This operation combines the effects of \( L_1 \) and \( L_2 \) on \( v \) linearly.

2. **The Function \( \text{func} \)**:
   - The function \( \text{func} \) takes a sum type as its argument, with two components: one corresponding to a function (here, \( f \)) and the other to the linear map (here, \( L_2 \)).
   - When applied to \( \text{Sum.inr } f \), \( \text{func} \) extracts and focuses solely on the component corresponding to \( f \).

3. **Applying \( \text{func} \) After the Sum**:
   - Applying \( \text{func} \) to \( (L_1 + L_2) \), \( M \), and \( \text{Sum.inr } f \) involves first combining \( L_1 \) and \( L_2 \), then applying \( \text{func} \) specifically to the \( f \) component.
   - Mathematically, this is represented as:
     \[
     \text{func} \left( \text{add } L_1 L_2 M \right) (\text{Sum.inr } f) (v) = \text{func}(f)(v)
     \]
     This equality suggests that \( \text{func} \) returns the same result regardless of whether \( L_1 \) and \( L_2 \) are added or not when accessing \( f \).

4. **Explanation of Equality**:
   - By the definition of the sum of linear maps, \( (L_1 + L_2)(v) = L_1(v) + L_2(v) \).
   - The \( \text{func} \) function, when applied to \( \text{Sum.inr } f \), focuses on \( f \) and completely ignores \( L_2 \) or any other components.
   - Therefore, the specific contributions of \( L_1 \) and \( L_2 \) to the result of \( (L_1 + L_2)(v) \) do not influence the outcome when \( \text{func} \) is applied to \( f \).

5. **Conclusion**:
   - Since \( \text{func} \) exclusively focuses on \( f \) and disregards the linear effects of \( L_1 \) and \( L_2 \), adding \( L_1 \) and \( L_2 \) does not affect the application of \( \text{func} \) to \( f \).
   - Hence, the equality holds:
     \[
     \text{func} \left( (L_1 + L_2) M \right) (\text{Sum.inr } f) = \text{func}(f)
     \]

informal_proof: By defining `ofFunc` with `func := fun _ f v => fF f v` and `rel := fun _ r _ => r.elim`, we ensure that functions and relations from the original structure are faithfully translated into the new context. The function `func` applies the corresponding function `fF` to the function `f` and value `v`, mirroring their usage. The relation `rel` utilizes `r.elim` to handle relations, ensuring that their eliminations are preserved. This construction guarantees that the behavior of functions and relations is maintained across the mapped structures.

informal_statement: The structure M is elementarily equivalent to itself within the class of all L-structures that include M. In other words, for any first-order sentence in the language L, M satisfies the sentence if and only if every L-structure that includes M as a substructure also satisfies the sentence.
informal_proof:
By definition, two structures are elementarily equivalent if they satisfy the same first-order sentences in the given language L. Since M is a structure in this language where all elements of L are included, the statement asserts that M is elementarily equivalent to itself. This means that for any sentence σ in L:

1. If σ is true in M, then it must also be true in every L-structure that includes M as a substructure.
2. Conversely, if σ is true in every such L-structure containing M, then it must also be true in M.

These two directions together confirm the equivalence, as they cover all possible interpretations within the specified class of structures.

informal_statement: For any language \( L \) and type \( M \), the models of \( L \) over \( M \) are naturally equivalent to \( M \) itself, where each model is constructed as a singleton set containing an element of \( M \).
informal_proof: To establish the equivalence between a type \( M \) and the set of models of a language \( L \) over \( M \), we define a function that maps each element of \( M \) to a model, which is a singleton set containing that element. Specifically, for every \( x \in M \), we map it to the model \(\{x\}\). Conversely, for each model \(\{x\}\), we map it back to the element \( x \). This ensures that applying the forward function followed by the inverse function brings us back to the original element, and vice versa. Therefore, the two mappings are consistent with the definitions of equivalence, confirming that the models of \( L \) over \( M \) are naturally equivalent to \( M \).
